abstract: VIP and NDNF positive interneurons are both found in layers 1 and 2/3 of the cortex, but have distinct patterns of gene expression, morphology, and connectivity. Despite this, their functional roles in the sensory cortices seem remarkably similar; their activity correlates with behavioral state, and they gate behaviorally driven increases in excitatory activity and sensory-driven responses. We sought to directly compare VIP and NDNF positive interneurons in the mouse visual cortex to determine if their activity was indeed functionally redundant or could be distinguished by their correlation to behavioral state, to excitatory activity, or to excitatory visual responses. Using simultaneous recordings of pupil diameter and running speed together with dual-population calcium imaging, we found that although the activity of both VIP and NDNF positive interneurons was more strongly correlated with behavior than was excitatory neuron activity, VIP positive interneuron activity was more strongly correlated with pupil diameter, whereas layer 2/3 NDNF positive interneuron activity was more strongly correlated with running speed. Excitatory-to-VIP pairwise correlation increased during locomotion, whereas excitatory-to-NDNF pairwise correlation decreased during locomotion. Intriguingly, although VIP-to-NDNF pairwise correlation was high, cortical depth significantly affected both VIP-to-NDNF correlation and the correlation of NDNF positive interneurons with pupil diameter and running speed. As expected, excitatory visual responses were significantly modulated by both pupil dilation and locomotion. However, we found that the level of VIP and NDNF activity preceding stimulus onset had a unique contribution to and was positively correlated with the amplitude of excitatory visual responses. Thus, while highly correlated to one another and to behavioral state, VIP and NDNF positive interneurons are functionally distinguishable in their relationship to both behavior and excitatory activity in the mouse visual cortex.
